data.title: Sending in certified record of proceedings
data.text:
(1) On receipt of an originating application for judicial review and a notice in accordance with rule 3.18 , the person or body named in the [Notice to obtain record of proceedings] notice must, as soon as practicable, (a) comply with the notice and send to the court clerk a certified record of proceedings in Form 9, or (b) provide in Form 9 a written explanation why the notice cannot be complied with or fully complied with.
(2) The certified record of proceedings sent to the court clerk under this rule constitutes part of the court file of the originating application.
(3) If the Court is not satisfied with the explanation for not sending all or part of the record of proceedings, the Court may order any or all of the following:
(a) the person or body to provide a better explanation;
(b) the person or body to send a certified copy of a record to the court clerk;
(c) the person or body to take any other action the Court considers appropriate.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.19 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text:
This rule works in conjunction with rule 3.18. It mandates the return of a Form 9 certified record of proceedings or an explanation as to why compliance is partially or fully impossible. The purpose is to obtain the record of what was before the decision-maker so that the court will have the same record as the basis for its review of the decision.
[2004] O.J. No. 4351 (Ont. Div. Ct.), when stating: “[a] record need not be produced if the body and act in question were not subject to judicial review and the time to make that determination was prior to the hearing of the full review application.”

data.title: Other circumstances when record of proceedings may be required
data.text:
(1) The Court may make an order for the production of the certified record of proceedings of a person or body if the conditions described in subrule (2) are met.
(2) The conditions are:
(a) the originating application for judicial review is for an order other than an order to set aside a decision or act;
(b) the certified record of proceedings is required to establish the claim;
(c) the person or body that is the subject of the originating application has not sent to the court clerk the certified record of proceedings within a reasonable time after the originating applicant’s written request for the person or body to do so.
(3) If the Court orders the certified record of proceedings to be sent to the court clerk, rules 3.18(3) and 3.19 [Notice to obtain record of proceedings]
[Sending in certified copy of record of proceedings] apply, unless the Court otherwise orders.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.20 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

data.title: Limit on questioning
data.text:
On an originating application for judicial review, no person may be questioned as a witness for the purpose of obtaining a transcript for use at the hearing without the Court’s permission.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.21 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text: This is a common sense rule, since the record, by the time the matter reaches a judicial review, is established. Presumptively, no additional evidence should be considered on review.

data.title: Stay of decision
data.text:
(1) The Court may stay the operation of a decision or act sought to be set aside under an originating application for judicial review pending final determination of the originating application.
(2) Despite subrule (1), no order to stay is to be made if, in the Court’s opinion, the stay would be detrimental either to the public interest or to public safety.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.23 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

data.title: Additional remedies on judicial review
data.text:
(1) If an originating applicant is entitled to a declaration that a decision or act of a person or body is unauthorized or invalid, the Court may, instead of making a declaration, set aside the decision or act.
(2) The Court may (a) direct a person or body to reconsider the whole or any part of a matter, (b) direct a person or body to reconsider the whole or any part of a decision if the Court has set aside the decision under subrule (1), and (c) give any other directions it considers necessary.
(3) If the sole ground for a remedy is a defect in form or a technical irregularity, the Court may, if the Court finds that no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice has occurred, despite the defect, (a) refuse a remedy, or (b) validate the decision made to have effect from a date and subject to any terms and conditions that the Court considers appropriate.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.24 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text:
This rule gives the court broad powers on judicial review to permit it to craft a remedy appropriate to the circumstances. Ordinarily, having found an administrative decision is unreasonable, the reviewing court should remit the matter for rehearing, unless, “. . . in light of the circumstances and the evidence in the record, only one interpretation or solution is possible, that is, where any other interpretation or solution would be unreason- able”, in which case the court may determine the matter on the merits.

data.title: Effect of not serving statement of claim in time
data.text:
If a statement of claim is not served on a defendant within the time or extended time for service, (a) no further proceeding may be taken in the action against a defendant who was not served in time, and (b) a statement of claim served on any defendant in time is unaffected by the failure to serve any other defendant in time.

commentary.topic: Limit on Service of Statement of Claim
commentary.text: Rule 3.28 imposes a strict and mandatory limit on the service of a statement of claim. Sanderson Estate v. Potter, [2012] A.J. No. 1014, 2012 ABQB 593 at para. 27 (Alta. Q.B.). If the statement of claim is not served in time, it is dead as against defendants not served Foster v. Robb, [2011] A.J. No. 1497, 2011 ABQB 776 at para. 6 (Alta. Q.B.). and a plaintiff’s only option is to commence a new proceeding by filing a new claim. Of course, if limitation periods have expired in the interim, that can affect the overall viability of such a “follow-up” claim.

data.title: Demand for notice by defendant
data.text:
(1) If the defendant files a demand for notice, the demand must be in Form 13.
(2) The defendant must file the demand for notice and serve it on the plaintiff within the applicable time after service of the statement of claim on the defendant.
(3) The applicable time is, (a) 20 days if service is effected in Alberta, (b) one month if service is effected outside Alberta but in Canada, and (c) 2 months if service is effected outside Canada.
(4) If the defendant files a demand for notice and serves it on the plaintiff, the defendant must be served with notice of any application or proceeding in which the defendant is named as respondent, but filing and service of the notice does not give the defendant a right to contest liability.
(5) If a defendant files a demand for notice and serves it on the plaintiff, the defendant may subsequently file a statement of defence only with the Court’s permission.
(6) Judgment or an order may be given against a defendant who has filed and served a demand for notice only if (a) the plaintiff applies to the Court for judgment or an order, and (b) notice of the application is served on the defendant.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.34 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

commentary.text:
An action in which a demand for notice is filed is partially defended. Swain v. McLachlan, [2016] A.J. No. 9, 2016 ABQB 8 at para. 10 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).
A defendant who files a demand for notice, in essence, admits liability on the terms alleged in the statement of claim. Richardson v. Richardson, [2018] A.J. No. 1177, 2018 ABCA 327 at para. 8 (Alta. C.A.). However, a demand for notice allows the defendant to challenge the quantum of the claim. Swain v. McLachlan, [2016] A.J. No. 9, 2016 ABQB 8 at para. 10 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).
A defendant who files a demand for notice cannot contest liability; however, he or she is entitled to notice of any application or proceeding in the action. Richardson v. Richardson, [2018] A.J. No. 1177, 2018 ABCA 327 at para. 8 (Alta. C.A.). Accordingly, the plaintiff A demand for notice is suited for use in rare, special circumstances. Most frequently, it is filed in response to mortgage foreclosure actions.

data.title: Judgment or order by agreement
data.text:
(1) If a lawyer files a statement of defence or demand for notice on behalf of a defendant, no judgment or order may be obtained by agreement of the parties unless the defendant’s lawyer of record is a party to the agreement or consents to the agreement.
(2) If a defendant (a) does not file a statement of defence or a demand for notice, (b) files a statement of defence or demand for notice in person or by a lawyer who has ceased to be the defendant’s lawyer of record, or (c) is not represented by a lawyer of record, no judgment or order may be obtained by agreement of the parties unless the defendant’s agreement, with an affidavit of execution, is filed with the application for the judgment or order.
(3) If a lawyer files a statement of claim on behalf of a plaintiff, no judgment or order may be obtained by agreement of the parties unless the plaintiff’s lawyer of record is a party to the agreement or consents to the agreement.
(4) If a plaintiff (a) files a statement of claim in person or by a lawyer who has ceased to be the plaintiff’s lawyer of record, or (b) is not represented by a lawyer of record, no judgment or order may be obtained by agreement of the parties unless the plaintiff’s agreement, with an affidavit of execution, is filed with the application for the judgment or order.

rules.title: Judgment for debt or liquidated demand
rules.text:
(1) If a statement of claim includes a claim for a debt or a liquidated demand, with or without interest, whether as debt or damages, and one or more defendants do not file a statement of defence or demand for notice in response to that claim or any part of it, the plaintiff (a) may enter judgment for a sum not exceeding the amount in respect of which no defence is filed and the interest payable, if the interest calculation is based on a set rate, either under an agreement or an enactment, and (b) is entitled to a costs award.
(2) In this rule, “liquidated demand” means (a) a claim for a specific sum payable under an express or implied contract for the payment of money, including interest, not being in the nature of a penalty or unliquidated damages, where the amount of money claimed can be determined by (i) the terms of the contract, (ii) calculation only, or (iii) taking an account between the plaintiff and the defendant, or (b) a claim for a specific sum of money, whether or not in the nature of a penalty or damages, recoverable under an enactment that contains R. 3.39 [Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.39 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]

commentary.text:
This rule permits the court (through the court clerk) to issue judgment for a debt or liquidated demand. This rule must be strictly complied with, or the court will refuse to enter judgment. See , [2015] A.J. No. 1092, 2015 ABQB 629 (Alta. Q.B.). Re Boisjoli This requires the pleadings in the statement of claim and the default judgment itself to comply. See , [2015] A.J. No. 1092, 2015 ABQB 629 (Alta. Q.B.). Re Boisjoli Interest, if claimed, must be specifically calculated in a schedule to the default judgment.
Under rule 3.39, default judgment is only available when the plaintiff sues for an exact, or easily calculable, amount. TLA Food Services Ltd. v. 1144707 Alberta Ltd., [2011] A.J. No. 975, 2011 ABQB 550 at para. For this reason, the statement of claim must be drafted very carefully, especially particulars of relief claimed, to enable the clerk to issue a default judgment as a mere clerical function, based only on the statement of claim and rudimentary calculations. If default judgment is refused, a plaintiff may still note the defendant in default pursuant to rule 3.36.
Judgment Against One Defendant Where Multiple Defendants – Rules 3.39 and 3.40 provide that where two parties are jointly liable and both are sued in one action but only one defends, the plaintiff may take default judgment and continue against the other. When this happens, the result (assuming the defended claim is successful in the end) is that there will be different judgments for different amounts, because contractual interest would continue to run against one debtor who defended but would stop as against the one against whom default proceedings were taken. On the defendant against whom default judgment is taken, interest thereafter accrues only under the Judgment Interest Act. Judgment Interest Act Domenic Construction Ltd. v. Primewest Capital , R.S.A. 2000, c. J-1; Corp., [2019] A.J. No. 108, 2019 ABQB 58 at para. 80 (Alta. Q.B.), revd (in part) on other grounds

rules.title: Continuation of action following judgment
rules.text:
If judgment is entered against some but not all defendants under (a) rule 3.36 , [Judgment in default of defence and noting in default]
(b) rule 3.37 [Application for judgment against defendant noted in default], (c) rule 3.38 , or [Judgment for recovery of property]
(d) rule 3.39 , [Judgment for debt or liquidated demand] the plaintiff may continue the action in respect of any defendant against whom judgment is not entered.

*[Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.40 effective November 1, 2010 (Alta. Gaz. August 14, 2010)]*

rules.title: Limitation on when judgment or noting in default may occur
rules.text:
Despite anything in this Division, judgment may not be entered against a defendant and a defendant may not be noted in default if the defendant has filed an application that has not been decided (a) to set aside service of a statement of claim, or (b) under rule 3.68 to [Court options to deal with significant deficiencies] set aside or amend a statement of claim, to strike out a claim, or to stay an action, application or proceeding.

rules.title: How to make claim against co-defendant
rules.text:
(1) If a defendant claims a contribution or indemnity, or both, against a co-defendant under the Tort- feasors Act Contributory Negligence Act or the , (a) the defendant may file and serve on a co-defendant a notice in Form 15 claiming a remedy under either or both of those Acts, (b) neither the defendant nor the co-defendant need file a pleading in respect of a claim or defence under those Acts unless the Court otherwise orders, and (c) a third party claim need not be filed and served on the co-defendant.
(2) The notice claiming contribution must be filed and served on the co-defendant within 20 days after the date on which the defendant files the statement of defence or demand for notice.
Karas v. Mongeon, [2018] A.J. No. 238, 2018 ABQB 149 at para. 6 (Alta. Q.B.).
